newsitem.title: UNITED NATIONS: Guatemala's rebels lobby China on U.N. mission.
newsitem.headline: Guatemala's rebels lobby China on U.N. mission.

text.p: Guatemalan rebel leaders came to New York on Friday to lobby China into approving a U.N. peacekeeping mission it vetoed because of Guatemala's ties to Taiwan.

Diplomats said two leaders of the leftist Guatemalan National Revolutionary Unit (URNG), known as Commander Gasper Ilon and Commander Tomas, met Chinese diplomats as well as envoys from the United States, Mexico, Spain, Colombia, Norway and Venezuela, who are guiding the peace process.

But so far, talks between China's U.N. ambassador Qin Huason and his Guatemalan counterpart, Julio Martini Herrera. which resumed on Friday, have not resulted in a change of policy by Beijing. The object of the talks is for China to reverse its Security Council vote and rescue the mission.

The guerrilla leaders are said to be more eager than the Guatemalan army to have U.N. observers in their country to verify peace accords signed on Dec. 29 after 36 years of civil war. Under the agreements, the army is to cut down its numbers and the guerrillas are to go to assembly points, disarm and be integrated into civilian life.

The 14 other Security Council members a week ago all supported sending the peacekeepers to Guatemala for a three-month period. But a negative vote by China, one of five permanent council members with veto power, killed the mission.

Diplomats said that China was not asking for a break in diplomatic relations between Guatemala and Taiwan as a condition for supporting the peacekeepers. But among its demands were that Guatemala stop supporting moves to put U.N. membership for Taiwan on the General Assembly's agenda.
Another, they said, was a public apology from Guatemala for inviting Taiwan's foreign minister, John Chang, to the Dec. 29 peace signing ceremonies. But Guatemala has refused to do this.

Taipei was expelled from the United Nations in 1971 and replaced by Beijing as the rightful representative of China. It has given generous economic aid to a host of small nations in Central America, the Caribbean and Africa.

Should the issue not be resolved next week in the Security Council, diplomats said Mexico and others have threatened to ask the 185-member General Assembly to approve the mission. The assembly has already established a nearly 500-strong human rights monitoring mission in Guatemala, which has a few military officers in its ranks.

But none of the council's five permanent members -- the United States, Britain, France, Russia and China -- are in favor of this move and do not want to give up any of their privileges to the 184-member assembly. For China, a likely defeat in the assembly would be a public embarrassment.
In Guatemala City, President Alvaro Arzu said on Friday the country could, if necessary, carry out the crucial military part of the accords without international observers.
Guatemala, he said, would also continue to explore the option of seeking an alternative group of monitors from the Organization of American States.
But diplomats said the OAS was not eager to carry out the task and that the URNG was insisting on the United Nations after years of brutal warfare with the army.
